title: Honor the character
hookLine: girls flattered for looks from fourteen should learn they're honored for self-respect (Enchiridion 40)

cards: Listen to what grown-ups say to children at a family party. To the little boys: you're so strong, you're so fast. To the little girls, again and again: look how pretty you are.
It's meant kindly. But children pick up what the adults around them value, often from exactly these small remarks.
Epictetus noticed the same thing in his own world, and wrote it down in a section of the handbook that's short, a little uncomfortable, and still sharp.

teach.b: In section forty, Epictetus says that from about fourteen, girls are flattered by men and called ladies.
Seeing that they're valued for nothing except their appeal to men, he says, they begin to dress up and put all their hopes in that.
His answer: it's worth taking care that they come to understand they're honored for nothing else than being decent and self-respecting. Not for looks. For character.
That's the whole section. An honest note.
It's written about girls, by a man, in a society that gave women little say over their own lives, and some modern readers find parts of its framing dated.
But the core sentence points a finger at the people doing the flattering as much as at the girls, and it says plainly that a young woman's worth is in her character.
Stoic teachers before him, like Musonius Rufus, Epictetus' own teacher, argued that women should study philosophy too. Why it reaches us: the praise people give teaches others what they're worth.

Praise only looks, and you teach someone to put their hopes in a mirror, which time will eventually disappoint. Praise honesty, kindness, courage, effort, and you point them at the part of themselves nobody can take away.
In Stoic terms, you praise what's up to them.
That works for boys, for adults, for anyone.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism make a habit of praising others, especially children, for character and effort rather than appearance, following Epictetus' point in Enchiridion 40.

games.q: honor the character — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says girls should focus on their looks
he says they should learn they're honored only for decency and self-respect.
Epictetus' own teacher argued women should study philosophy

games.q: your niece shows you a drawing she worked on all afternoon, in a new dress. what fits Enchiridion 40?
o: you stuck with that all afternoon. tell me about it.
games.why: he says people should learn they're honored for character, not looks. praise what was up to her.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'll see soon, a child, a friend, a coworker, a partner, and set aside how they look.

Ask instead what you've seen in their character lately: patience with a hard customer, honesty when it cost something, kindness nobody else noticed. Find one, and the plain words you'd use to name it.

wordCard.voice: Musonius Rufus. Epictetus' own teacher, who argued that women should study philosophy too; people should be honored for decency and self-respect, not looks. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: self-respect, a sense of shame in the good sense. Enchiridion 40 uses the related adjective.

carryVoice: Your line: nobody can take away. It just takes a little more attention than noticing a haircut. See you tomorrow.
